title: My sons, and Pandu's
hookLine: a blind king asks what happened on the battlefield, and one small word, mine, gives him away
tomorrow: a warrior drops his bow. what does he say next?
last: I AM, YOU ARE, IT IS.

lines: A BLIND KING IN A PALACE.
MY SONS, AND THE SONS OF PANDU.
cards: A palace in Hastinapura, and a war about to begin outside it. Out on the field, conch shells are about to sound. The old king, Dhritarashtra, can't see.
In the Mahabharata's telling, the sage Vyasa has given his advisor Sanjaya the sight to watch the battlefield from far away and report it. So the king asks.

His words open the Bhagavad Gita: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered and eager to fight, my sons and the sons of Pandu, what did they do? Listen again to how he names them. My sons.

teach.b: The Sanskrit is mamakah pandavash chaiva. Mamakah: mine, my own, from mama, my. Pandavah: the sons of Pandu.
Chaiva: and also. Now what a reader notices.
Pandu was the king's own brother. The Pandavas are his nephews, raised in his house. A plain word for family was right there.
Instead he reaches for mamakah, mine, and sets the others beside it: Pandu's. Two sides, before a single arrow.
Remember the verse from two days ago: this one is mine, that one is a stranger's, is how the narrow-hearted count. The king's first question counts exactly that way.
That's the answer to yesterday's riddle: the word that gives him away is mine. And this is a real thread in Hindu teaching, not just a sad detail.
The tradition names the feeling: mamata, mine-ness, and it sits right beside ahankara, the I-maker, the ego.
The Gita answers its own first question in its second chapter: the one who moves through life without longing, nirmama, without mine, nirahankara, without the I-maker, finds peace.

teach.h: THE BOOK OPENS ON THE KNOT IT UNTIES.
teach.b: So the book opens on the very knot it spends seven hundred verses untying. Many teachers read the king's blindness the same way: he can't see the field, and he can't see past mine.

how: The Bhagavad Gita opens with Dhritarashtra's question to Sanjaya, and students reading it in Sanskrit often begin at this first verse; in the Vedic fire offering, many Hindus say idam na mama, this is not mine, with each oblation.

games.why: the king's first word for his sons is mamakah, mine, set against "the sons of Pandu." the Gita calls that mine-ness a knot, and says peace comes without "i" and "mine."

practice: In the Vedic fire offering, with each spoonful poured into the flame, the words come: idam na mama. This is not mine. Look at one thing near you that you'd call mine: a mug, a phone, a jacket.
Notice how the word mine feels. If you pray, say silently, idam na mama, this is not mine, and offer it. If you don't, simply let the word go, and just see the thing.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words, the plain ones that keep returning. Today, mama, my, and mamakah, mine: the word in the Gita's first question, and na mama, not mine, the word said into the sacred fire.
